title: Summarise board minutes with cited output to focus risk identification
problem: Auditors read board minutes and similar documents to spot risk indicators, but the volume is large, reading it all is slow, and relevant passages are easy to miss.
approach: KPMG describes Clara AI assistants that review documents such as minutes to flag possible risks, announced for 90,000 auditors in July 2024.
The FRC's worked example for a hypothetical firm has the tool summarise each meeting, with every point citing its source.
The auditor reads the minutes to check completeness and accuracy; KPMG gives no usage, accuracy or time figure (self-reported).
The Dutch regulator AFM says nearly all firms it visited use generative AI, for example to summarise minutes, without naming them.

title: Chat assistants for entity research and methodology questions during planning
problem: Building an understanding of the entity, its industry and its regulatory environment takes desk research and document reading, and auditors spend time finding firm-approved guidance.
approach: KPMG reported more than 2.175 million Audit Chat conversations since October 2023 (self-reported); this is usage, not effect.
RSM's Ask Luca answers questions grounded in firm-approved guidance and, RSM says, reduces research time (self-reported); PwC describes ChatNational.
The auditor owns the understanding of the entity: ICAEW found chatbots cannot perform inquiry, observation or inspection; RSM calls human review vital.

title: Agents that scan media reports for emerging threats and draft staff memos
problem: Keeping up with news and events that bear on an audited entity's risk is manual and uneven.
approach: Bloomberg Law reports Deloitte auditors worldwide gained agents that scan media reports for emerging threats and produce first drafts of staff memos.
Deloitte describes an agent network in Omnia for nearly 85,000 practitioners, running preliminary procedures for review.
Practitioners supervise and validate agent output; a Deloitte leader expects faster working-paper population, an expectation not a result (self-reported).

title: Analyse audit-committee communications to surface issues earlier in audit preparation
problem: Issues raised in communications with the audit committee can reach the engagement team late in the audit preparation cycle.
approach: PwC said in October 2026 that one tool it will use for 2026 year-end audits analyses audit-committee communications to surface issues sooner.
No outcome is published and the human checkpoint is not described in the source.

title: Tool-assisted understanding of the client's IT environment and access rights
problem: Understanding the entity's IT environment is required in risk assessment, but sampling user lists and access logs gives a partial picture, and mid-tier firms often lack IT audit teams.
approach: The Dutch regulator AFM saw auditors using tools to evaluate access rights and user activity; these are analytics tools, not necessarily AI.
A vendor co-founder writes that agentic AI platforms can map risks to controls and draft ISA 315 documentation with human-in-the-loop review.
Auditors review, validate and challenge flagged issues and evaluate tool results against the IT auditor's findings. No outcome is published.
who: AFM, ICAEW viewpoint by a vendor co-founder

title: Idea: understand the entity's AI use as a standard risk assessment step
problem: Idea, not a deployment: audit partners rated only 6% of their largest clients' AI governance as advanced, yet the AS 2110 text has no AI-specific step.
approach: Planning would add inquiry into how the entity uses AI in financial reporting, its governance, and whether AI-generated documents feed audit evidence.
The AICPA practice aid (13 October 2026) covers AI-specific risks and controls; this is guidance, not yet a measured practice.
The auditor remains responsible for the audit and the opinion, in the AICPA chief auditor's words; no firm has published results.

title: Standardised ERP data ingestion as the base for planning analytics
problem: Fragmented tools and client data in many formats block analytics at the start of the audit; surveyed US firms name poor client data (60%) among the top blockers.
approach: Grant Thornton's gtap is a cloud platform standardising how audit data from any ERP system is ingested, transformed and analysed.
It supports full-population analysis, started with private-company audits, and plans public companies the next year.
Auditors oversee the risks and anomalies agents flag; Grant Thornton says consistency rises and manual steps fall, with no figure (self-reported).
Adoption signal: 35% of surveyed US firms have automated trial-balance import and 19% automated data ingestion (independent).

title: Whole-population ledger analytics to identify risks and unusual flows
problem: Planning often starts from a trial balance, a few schedules, last year's file and judgment, so significant classes and unexpected flows can stay hidden until costlier substantive testing.
approach: RSM auditors review journal-entry visualisations for risk insight, and KPMG says Clara Transaction Scoring covers 100% of populations.
The auditor interprets results and follows up outliers; senior team members reflect on whether scepticism was maintained.
Adoption signal, not quality: 55% of IFIAR members frequently observed automated tools in risk assessment in 2024, 49% in 2023 (independent).
22% of US firms have an automated risk-assessment solution; every respondent using one reported positive impact (independent).

title: Draft engagement-specific risk suggestions from trial balance, prior-year file and board minutes
problem: Risk assessment starts from a blank page or from last year's risks, and is time-consuming, according to a customer.
approach: Caseware's Risk Suggestion Agent, launched 6 October 2026, suggests engagement-specific risks with a rationale from financial data and board minutes.
The auditor accepts, edits or rejects every suggestion; nothing enters the engagement file without a deliberate decision.
In a demonstration it surfaced 5 risks, one a $118,000 discrepancy with board minutes (vendor-published).
A GRF CPAs & Advisors partner says it saves time, with no figure (vendor-published).

title: Agentic risk assessment linking evidence, analytics, assertions, materiality and planned procedures
problem: Risk scores from analytics often sit outside workpaper tools and are hard to tie to assertions and materiality, and linking risks to procedures is manual.
approach: MindBridge announced Agentic Risk Assessment on 22 September 2026, connecting evidence, analytics, assertions, materiality and methodology to support planning decisions.
Wolters Kluwer describes a future-state vision where agents draft a cited risk narrative and map risks to procedures, with the auditor reviewing.
The auditor reviews and refines the output; MindBridge claims better planning decisions, with no figure and no named customer (vendor-published).

title: Large-firm agent platforms covering planning and risk identification
problem: Separate point tools leave planning, risk assessment and testing disconnected, so risk views are not updated as work proceeds.
approach: EY embedded a multi-agent framework in EY Canvas on 7 April 2026, with end-to-end support expected by 2028.
Deloitte says Omnia agents identify potential risk factors; KPMG Clara GenAI helps refine risk assessments; PwC expects an agentic platform.
Practitioners supervise and validate agent output; preliminary conclusions go to professionals for review.
EY reports reach of 130,000 professionals and 160,000 engagements (self-reported): reach, not effect.
who: EY, Deloitte, KPMG, PwC, Grant Thornton

title: Idea: chatbot drafts risks of material misstatement from financial statements (weak results)
problem: Idea, not a deployment: identifying risks of material misstatement takes time, and a general-purpose chatbot can produce a polished draft in seconds.
approach: ICAEW tested Copilot, Claude Sonnet 4 and Grok 3 once each on a fictional retailer; the case for chatbots was not made.
None of three performed risk assessment as a human auditor would; 0 of 3 separated statement-level from assertion-level risks (independent).
Reports took from under 20 seconds to about 3.5 minutes (independent); Copilot did not treat revenue as a risk area.
ICAEW concludes human judgement is needed to interpret the output and decide the risks, because each model gave different answers.

title: Idea: multi-agent restatement-risk scoring from report text, ratios and audit matters
problem: Idea, not a deployment: entity-level risk signals come from several evidence streams that can disagree, and point predictions say nothing about how well the streams agree.
approach: A research preprint describes UMAR: three agents score risk from report text, financial ratios and audit matters, each with an uncertainty estimate.
An aggregator combines the scores and measures conflict between agents; the authors call the output potentially actionable and interpretable.
On the authors' test set it beat logistic regression, XGBoost and FinBERT: AUROC 0.782, calibration error 0.052 (independent). Human checkpoint not described.

title: GenAI as a sounding board in fraud risk assessment and fraud brainstorming
problem: Fraud risk assessment is vulnerable to cognitive bias, such as irrelevant information diluting relevant indicators, and brainstorming depends on the team's knowledge of schemes elsewhere.
approach: The AFM reports auditors at unnamed Dutch firms making their own fraud risk assessment first, then using GenAI to challenge it.
A City of Charlotte internal auditor showed a chatbot drafting a table of cemetery fraud schemes; the slides show no review step.
Conference experiment with irrelevant information added: ratings 8.00 vs 6.42 without ChatGPT, 8.91 vs 7.97 with it (independent).
No outcome is published for the practitioner demonstration.
who: AFM, City of Charlotte auditor, Tilburg University

title: Idea: extend fraud risk assessment to AI-enabled schemes and AI-generated evidence
problem: Idea, not a deployment: documents such as invoices and bank statements may now originate from or be altered by AI, which traditional fraud risk factors do not cover.
approach: The fraud risk assessment and team discussion would add AI-enabled schemes such as deepfake impersonation in wire authorisations and fabricated invoices.
Teams would consider whether AI algorithms initiate accounting entries and plan authenticity checks where document authenticity is in doubt.
The engagement team discusses with the engagement partner as the human checkpoint.
Survey of 373 internal audit leaders: 85% rate AI-enabled fraud a moderate to high risk; 62% unprepared or minimally prepared (independent).

title: Idea: chatbot proposes the materiality benchmark, percentage and performance materiality
problem: Idea, not a deployment: setting overall and performance materiality needs a benchmark, a percentage and a rationale, and inspectors scrutinise year-on-year changes.
approach: ICAEW asked three chatbots to calculate materiality with a rationale in one test; no source describes AI setting materiality in practice.
The models proposed different benchmarks for the same facts: Claude 5% of profit before tax, Copilot 0.75% of revenue (independent).
Copilot's rationale may be a hallucination; ICAEW concludes human judgement is required to choose the benchmark and thresholds.

title: AI-supported scoping decisions, including group components
problem: Deciding which accounts, processes, locations and components are in scope is a judgment call made largely from prior-year files and team knowledge, and group audits are among the hardest.
approach: PwC said in October 2025 it planned soon to have a scoping risk-assessment tool; its October 2026 follow-up does not mention it.
Wolters Kluwer says automation and AI can consolidate group data and prioritise exceptions; it describes no component-scoping method and names no customer.
A person decides scope: PwC says the tool will help people make smarter decisions; auditors evaluate AI-flagged results. No outcome published.

title: Auto-populate the planning document from prior-year information and show what changed
problem: Planning documents are rebuilt each year from prior-year files, and auditors may not notice what has changed in the business.
approach: PwC's Simplified Audit for Private Business ingests prior-year information and auto-populates a planning document; 2025 was its first year in planning.
PwC says it saves time and helps auditors ask better questions by showing what changed (self-reported); no figure is published.
The document is a foundation for the auditor to consider; planning judgments stay with the team; no review steps are described.
PwC describes AI time savings across its audit tools as not that drastic yet (self-reported).

title: In-file assistant that checks the planning file for gaps at planning review
problem: Gaps in the risk assessment, such as a variance no logged risk covers, are often found during fieldwork rather than at planning review.
approach: In a Caseware CwX 2026 demonstration, the Verity agent flagged a variance against board minutes with no logged risk attached.
The reviewer accepts, edits or rejects each suggestion before anything enters the engagement.
Caseware reports early beta cut manual workflows from 15-20 minutes to under two (vendor-published); not specific to planning review.
Caseware reports 94% accuracy on golden-dataset items (vendor-published); not specific to planning.

title: Methodology-embedded, risk-based engagement platform with in-context AI guidance for mid-tier firms
problem: Mid-tier firms use disconnected tools and prior-year habits, and some surveyed firms say they still struggle to move from prior-year workpapers to a risk-driven approach.
approach: EisnerAmper, Citrin Cooperman and PKF O'Connor Davies adopted the Dynamic Assurance Solution risk-focused suite, now with Caseware Verity.
PKF also joined an agentic pioneer programme to co-develop its own agents; EisnerAmper phased its roll-out with training.
Caseware says every AI-assisted output is citation-backed, reviewable and traceable before entering the engagement file.
Adoption, not an AI effect: more than 1,100 EisnerAmper professionals and over 1,500 engagements on the platform (vendor-published).
who: EisnerAmper, Citrin Cooperman, PKF O'Connor Davies, Caseware

title: Engagement-level plan for AI and tool use, with team competence checked
problem: Tools are adopted ad hoc, it is not always clear where GenAI was applied in an audit, and teams may use tools they are not trained for.
approach: The audit plan states which tools will be used for which risks; the team's competence to use them is assessed at planning.
The AFM saw audit plans at some firms stating which tools are used; the AICPA practice aid recommends planning intended AI use.
The engagement leader sets expectations at the outset; senior team members review overall technology use in the file. No outcome published.

title: AI-supported staffing requests, budget planning and engagement-leader review
problem: Manual staffing and budgeting processes give leaders little visibility into engagement planning and resourcing.
approach: RSM Luca Resourcing replaces manual processes with a connected tool supporting initial staffing requests, budget planning and engagement-leader review.
RSM presents it as one of three AI-related additions to its audit ecosystem; what the AI does inside is not stated.
Engagement-leader review of staffing and budget is a step in the tool; RSM says it improves visibility and speeds staffing decisions (self-reported).

title: AI efficiency gains negotiated into audit fees and engagement budgets
problem: If firms tell clients AI cuts hours, clients may ask why fees do not fall.
approach: Reported case: KPMG International pressed auditor Grant Thornton UK for a lower fee, arguing AI should cut audit cost; the fee fell.
Reported fee about 14% lower, $416,000 (2024) to $357,000 (2025); second-hand and unconfirmed (independent).
PwC said in 2025 clients know AI saves hours and ask for discounts; practitioners disagree on whether quality should support higher fees.
The human checkpoint is not described in the source.
who: KPMG International, Grant Thornton UK, PwC

title: Continuous risk assessment and dynamic planning that update risks as data arrives
problem: Risk assessment is a point-in-time planning step revised only when the team notices contradicting evidence, although AS 2110 .74 requires it to continue through the audit.
approach: Direction of travel, not yet practice: Thomson Reuters says client transactions flow continuously into AI engines that flag issues as they occur.
Grant Thornton designed gtap as the foundation for such a model, and Caseware's long-term aim includes AI that continuously assists planning.
The engagement team decides whether to revise the risk assessment; auditor intervention protocols apply when anomalies appear.
Thomson Reuters claims 80-90% complete deliverables by year-end with minimal human intervention (vendor-published); the claim is unsourced.

title: AI-drafted risk considerations, risk-to-control scoping and work programs for internal audit
problem: Internal audit teams plan many diverse audits with limited staff, and mapping risks to controls by hand before testing starts is where teams lose the most time.
approach: Helvetia Baloise's chief audit executive says the team uses AI to support audit work programs and summarise reports and policies.
Fieldguide's Field Agents map risks to controls and score them for a scoped starting point; BDO's risk advisory practice is rolling out.
The auditor reviews the scoping result and makes the final call; severity ratings, materiality calls and sign-off stay with people.
FJ Management's head of internal audit states a vision of an agent planning procedures and drafting workpapers for review; no outcome published.
who: Helvetia Baloise, Fieldguide, BDO, FJ Management
